method: The azimuthal equidistant projection puts one chosen point at the centre of a circular map and keeps two properties there: every other point is drawn at its true great-circle distance and on its true initial bearing, so the radial scale is exactly 1 and a straight line out of the centre is a great-circle track. The page places the point at x = rho sin(theta) east and y = rho cos(theta) north of the centre, where rho = R c is the great-circle distance for an angular distance c and theta is the initial azimuth. The angular distance comes from the haversine form, c = 2 atan2(sqrt(a), sqrt(1 - a)) with a = sin^2(dphi/2) + cos(phi1) cos(phi) sin^2(dlambda/2), which stays accurate for the metre-scale separations where the usual arccos(sin phi1 sin phi + cos phi1 cos phi cos dlambda) form loses precision; the change of longitude is wrapped into -180 to 180 degrees first, so a pair that straddles the antimeridian needs no special sign. The bearing is theta = atan2(sin dlambda cos phi, cos phi1 sin phi - sin phi1 cos phi cos dlambda) in degrees clockwise from true north. The sphere radius is R = 6371.0088 km, the IUGG mean radius, so distances are spherical great-circle distances and not geodesics on the WGS 84 ellipsoid, which differ by up to about 0.3 percent. Distortion away from the centre is purely tangential: the scale around the centre is k = c / sin c, about 1.0066 at 1,000 km, 1.0689 at 4,000 km, 1.2747 at 7,500 km, 1.5696 at 10,007 km (a quarter of the circumference), 1.9795 at 12,000 km and 3.3237 at 15,000 km, and the page reports that factor, the stretch it implies and the band it falls in: under 10,000 km close to a globe, 10,000 to 15,000 km visibly distorted, beyond 15,000 km severe. The antipode cannot be drawn: every azimuth is valid there and its image is the whole circle of radius pi R = 20,015.1 km, so the page reports that distance with no easting, northing, azimuth or scale instead of inventing an angle, and a point within a few metres of the antipode is treated the same way because the haversine no longer resolves the direction. A point that coincides with the centre returns zero distance, no bearing and a scale of 1. Latitudes are limited to plus or minus 90 degrees and longitudes to plus or minus 180 degrees, decimal commas and a leading plus are accepted, and the projection is spherical with no ellipsoid, datum shift or false easting; the page computes one point rather than drawing the map or a graticule.

sources.title: Azimuthal equidistant projection - all points are at proportionally correct distances from the centre point and at the correct azimuth from it, the projected radius is the great-circle arc length, cos(rho/R) = sin(phi0) sin(phi) + cos(phi0) cos(phi) cos(lambda - lambda0) with tan(theta) = cos(phi) sin(lambda - lambda0) / (cos(phi0) sin(phi) - sin(phi0) cos(phi) cos(lambda - lambda0)), the maximum plotted distance is half the circumference at about 20,000 km, distortion is minimal under 10,000 km, moderate between 10,000 and 15,000 km and severe beyond, the antipode smears into a whole circle, and a polar centre reduces to rho = R (pi/2 - phi) and theta = lambda
